## Numbers 34 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

Numbers 34 falls in the final section of the book (chs. 26–36), where the new generation is being prepared to enter Canaan. The chapter has two parts: the boundaries of the Promised Land (vv. 1–15) and the appointment of leaders to distribute it (vv. 16–29). As Ronald Allen puts it, "This chapter is a celebration of God's gifting, a liturgy of geography. It presents a trust deed, a legal document from God to his people." (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 1–2 — The Charge to Define the Borders

**v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses…"**
The divine initiative is stressed. These words would have been deeply encouraging to Israel on the plains of Moab: by giving detailed borders, God was assuring them of successful conquest. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 2: "When you enter the land of Canaan, it will be allotted to you as an inheritance with these boundaries…"**

- The phrase "shall fall to you" (KJV) uses the Hebrew verb *naphal* ("to fall"), a colourful reference to the casting of lots by which the land would be distributed — but the lot itself would be the outworking of God's will. The same wording appears in Judges 18:1, Psalm 16:6, and Ezekiel 47:14. (preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com)
- The land is described as an **inheritance**, not wages. Inheritances are freely given, not earned. Israel would have to conquer it, yet never think they earned it. (enduringword.com)
- Matthew Poole gave **three reasons** God detailed the boundaries: (1) to prevent Israel from expanding their empire like other nations — they were to be content with their own portion; (2) to encourage them in conquest and assure them of success; (3) to guide the coming distribution of the land. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)
- Ellicott adds that it was important for Israel to learn that, although divinely commissioned to exterminate the idolatrous Canaanites, they had **no commission to make aggressive wars** on surrounding nations beyond the allotted land. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/34.htm)
- John Currid notes that this chapter resembles an ancient Near-Eastern royal land grant: a king (Yahweh) granting land to a vassal (Israel), with specific boundaries — a common feature of ancient covenants. (preceptaustin.org)
- The NET Bible renders it: "the land that has been assigned to you as an inheritance." (preceptaustin.org)
- Matthew Henry observes that Canaan as bounded here was only about **160 miles long and 50 miles wide**, yet this was the vineyard of the Lord; the narrowness of space was made up by fruitfulness of soil. Those who have their portion in heaven have reason to be content with a small pittance of this earth. (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 3–5 — The Southern Border

**v. 3: "Your southern border will extend from the Wilderness of Zin along the border of Edom. On the east, your southern border will run from the end of the Salt Sea…"**

- The southern boundary is the same as that given for the tribe of Judah in Joshua 15:1–2. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- The border starts at the southern tip (or "tongue") of the Salt Sea (Dead Sea) and goes toward the Wilderness of Zin, which separated Israelite territory from Edom. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/; preceptaustin.org)
- Keil & Delitzsch explain that "on the sides of Edom" (Hebrew *al-yedei*) indicates contact along a long distance — the desert of Zin stretched along the side of Edom, and Canaan was separated from Edom by it. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-34.html)

**v. 4: "…cross south of the Ascent of Akrabbim, continue to Zin, and go south of Kadesh-barnea. Then it will go on to Hazar-addar and proceed to Azmon…"**

- The "Ascent of Akrabbim" means "Scorpion Pass." It is mentioned also in Joshua 15:3 and Judges 1:36. It was a well-known landmark — a winding road from the Nahal Zin basin into the Negeb, still known by that name through the Roman period and even today. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)
- Ellicott identifies it as a row of white cliffs running obliquely across the Arabah, about eight miles from the Dead Sea. The boundary line went south-westerly from the southern tongue of the Dead Sea to these heights, then westerly to Kadesh-barnea. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- The inclusion of **Kadesh-barnea** is striking — this was where the Israelite scouts first entered Canaan (Num 13:26) and where Israel had their long desert sojourn. "So close and yet so far!" as Precept Austin notes. There was a sense in which all those years at Kadesh, they were living on the very fringe of the land. (preceptaustin.org)

**v. 5: "…where it will turn from Azmon, join the Brook of Egypt, and end at the Sea."**

- The "Brook of Egypt" is not the Nile but the **Wadi el-Arish**, a seasonal watercourse that empties into the Mediterranean. This is the same as the southern boundary of Judah in Joshua 15:4. (preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- JFB identifies it as the ancient brook Sihor, the Rhinocolura of the Greeks, a little south of El-Arish. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)
- The boundary ran along valleys that form a natural division between cultivated land and desert, from the Arabah on the east to the Mediterranean on the west. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)

---

### v. 6 — The Western Border

**v. 6: "Your western border will be the coastline of the Great Sea; this will be your boundary on the west."**

- The **Great Sea** is the Mediterranean. There is no uncertainty about this border — it is universally acknowledged. It is called "great" in comparison with the small inland lakes known to the Hebrews. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)
- A question is whether Israel ever actually extended to this sea in the south — did they ever fully conquer the Philistines? David conquered them but did not exterminate them. At various times Israel lived among the Philistines. (preceptaustin.org, citing Gilbrant)

---

### vv. 7–9 — The Northern Border

**v. 7: "Your northern border will run from the Great Sea directly to Mount Hor…"**

- This **Mount Hor** is **not** the mountain where Aaron died (Num 20:22–27; 33:37–39). That was in the south near Edom. This is another peak by the same name, probably in the Lebanon range. (preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com)
- Ellicott notes that Hermon stands too far eastward to fit, and some peak very near the Mediterranean must be meant — possibly a peak of the Lebanon range visible from Sidon. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- JFB explains the Hebrew *Hor-ha-Hor* properly means "the mountain of the mountain" or "the high double mountain" — likely Mount Amana, a member of the great Lebanon range (Song 4:8). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)

**v. 8: "…from Mount Hor to Lebo-hamath, then extend to Zedad…"**

- "Lebo-hamath" (or "the entrance of Hamath") is probably modern Lebweh. It became the northern boundary of the Israelite kingdom under David and Solomon (1 Kings 8:65). (enduringword.com)
- JFB identifies "entrance of Hamath" as the northern plain between the mountain ranges, now the valley of Baalbek. Zedad is identified as modern Sudud. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)
- Hamath was a kingdom and city; the reference here is probably to the kingdom, since the city of Hamath never belonged to Israel. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-34.html — Constable)

**v. 9: "…continue to Ziphron, and end at Hazar-enan. This will be your boundary on the north."**

- Ziphron and Hazar-enan ("village of fountains") are unknown. The northern border is the most obscure of all four borders because so many sites are unidentified. (preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com, citing Wenham)
- The northern boundary fell well north of the northern border of modern Israel — north of ancient Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos. (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 10–12 — The Eastern Border

**v. 10: "And your eastern border will run straight from Hazar-enan to Shepham…"**

- The eastern border starts southward from the eastern point of the northern border (Hazar-enan) and extends south on an uncertain line. Shepham cannot be located with certainty. (enduringword.com, citing Wenham)

**v. 11: "…then go down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain and continue along the slopes east of the Sea of Chinnereth."**

- **Riblah** here must be distinguished from the Riblah in the land of Hamath (mentioned in 2 Kings 23:33; Jer 39:9). Ain (Hebrew for "fountain") is thought to be the great fountain of Neba Anjar at the foot of Antilibanus. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- **Sea of Chinnereth** is the Sea of Galilee. The name Chinnereth (or Cinnereth) probably derives from *kinnor*, "a harp," perhaps because of the lake's harp-like shape. In later times the city became Genusar, giving us "Gennesareth" in the Gospels. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- Keil & Delitzsch explain that the boundary "pressed upon the shoulder of the lake of Chinnereth toward the east" — i.e., the north-east shore of the Sea of Galilee. The border ran along the Jordan down to the Salt Sea. Hermon itself (Jebel es-Sheikh) did not belong to the land of Israel. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-34.html)

**v. 12: "Then the border will go down along the Jordan and end at the Salt Sea. This will be your land, defined by its borders on all sides."**

- The eastern border follows the Jordan River southward and ends at the Dead Sea. The line being drawn on the east of the river and the seas included those waters within the territory of the western tribes. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)

---

### vv. 13–15 — The Nine and a Half Tribes

**v. 13: "So Moses commanded the Israelites, 'Apportion this land by lot as an inheritance…'"**

- The land was to be divided **by lot**, so that each tribe would be satisfied with its possession as appointed by God's special providence. Its boundaries were fixed on divine authority to prevent covetousness after the territories of others. (enduringword.com, citing Clarke)
- The lot was not chance but the outworking of God's will (cf. Prov 16:33). (preceptaustin.org)
- "This was a wonderful and prosperous land, but in comparison with other places in the world, there was much it did not have, and God expected His people to be content with what He allotted to them." (enduringword.com, citing Watson)

**v. 14–15: "For the tribes of the Reubenites and Gadites, along with the half-tribe of Manasseh, have already received their inheritance… across the Jordan from Jericho, toward the sunrise."**

- The two and a half tribes had already chosen and received their inheritance east of the Jordan (Numbers 32). G. Campbell Morgan notes the repetition: "Thrice over the words are repeated in reference to them, they 'have received.' They had made their own choice and it was now ratified." (enduringword.com)
- Ellicott clarifies that "on this side Jordan" is better rendered "along the side or bank of Jordan." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)

---

### vv. 16–17 — Joshua and Eleazar Appointed

**v. 16–17: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'These are the names of the men who are to assign the land as an inheritance for you: Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun.'"**

- The division of land was potentially an explosive, divisive issue. God therefore called for the two most capable, godly, and prominent leaders — the spiritual leader (Eleazar) and the military leader (Joshua) — to supervise this controversial duty. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)
- John Trapp sees a Christological pointer: Eleazar the high priest points to "the High Priest of the new covenant, by whom we have entrance into the promised inheritance, whither he is gone before to prepare a place for us." (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)
- Matthew Henry remarks: "So sure must they feel of victory and success while God fought for them, that the persons are named who should be intrusted with the dividing of the land." (preceptaustin.org)

---

### vv. 18–29 — The Tribal Leaders

**v. 18: "Appoint one leader from each tribe to distribute the land."**

- In addition to Eleazar and Joshua, one chief man (prince) from each of the ten tribes that would settle in Canaan was chosen. This mirrored the pattern at the first census (Num 1:4) and ensured equity and impartiality in the allotment. The position of the territory only — not its dimensions — was determined by lot, while these leaders oversaw the fair distribution among families within each tribe. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/)
- Constable notes these were evidently not the heads of the tribes but men chosen specifically for this purpose. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-34.html)
- Gill adds that Reuben and Gad had no representatives because they already had their inheritance, and Levi had none because they were to have no territorial inheritance. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/34.htm — from search excerpt)

**v. 19: "Caleb son of Jephunneh from the tribe of Judah…"**

- Caleb is the only familiar name. He is the same faithful spy who, along with Joshua, brought a good report of the land 40 years earlier. God had promised him: "My servant Caleb… I will bring into the land which he entered, and his descendants shall take possession of it" (Num 14:24). His appearance here is the fulfillment of that promise. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)

**vv. 20–28:** The remaining nine leaders are listed — Shemuel (Simeon), Elidad (Benjamin), Bukki (Dan), Hanniel (Manasseh), Kemuel (Ephraim), Eli-zaphan (Zebulun), Paltiel (Issachar), Ahihud (Asher), and Pedahel (Naphtali). None of these names appears elsewhere in Scripture. The tribes are listed in rough order of their settlements, beginning with Judah and Simeon in the south and ending with Asher and Naphtali in the north (cf. Joshua 14–19). (enduringword.com, citing Wenham)

**v. 29: "These are the ones whom the LORD commanded to apportion the inheritance to the Israelites in the land of Canaan."**

- The chapter ends with a report of accomplishment: "These are the men." Ronald Allen notes: "These are the names of the second generation; the leaders of the earlier listings were now dead. But with the outlines of the land now in mind, and with new leaders of the tribes now in place, certainly soon the new generation will begin its long-anticipated conquest of the land under the hand of God." (preceptaustin.org)
- The actual division was later carried out at Shiloh, before the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle (Joshua 19:51). (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ — from search excerpt)

---

### Key Theological and Interpretive Points

#### The Borders Given vs. the Borders Promised to Abraham

Several commentators note a significant difference between the borders here and those promised to Abraham in Genesis 15:18–21 (which extended to the River Euphrates). Thomas Constable explains that the Numbers 34 borders were "not the same territory promised to Abraham but was what God gave the Israelites at their entrance into the land. If they had been obedient to Him, He would have eventually enlarged their borders to include the whole area promised to Abraham." Israel never fully possessed even the Numbers 34 borders — "on any estimate and interpretation, the 'Canaan' that was the inheritance given to Israel was larger and more extensive than they were ever able to possess, even in David's and Solomon's time." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-34.html)

#### Application for Believers

- **Contentment**: As Israel was given clear boundaries and expected to be content, "we should rest in the specific lot God has assigned us and resist the temptation to reach beyond the bounds of our own calling." (enduringword.com)
- **Failure to possess**: Precept Austin draws a parallel with NT believers who fail to "lay hold of all of the 'precious and magnificent promises' we have been granted by God (2 Peter 1:4). Why do so many fall so short? The answer is failure to obey the 'instruction manual' (AKA 'THE BIBLE')." (preceptaustin.org)
- **God-given limits**: F.B. Meyer reflected that God-given limits are not punishments but wise borders that define our true territory — "Take possession of every inch of God-given territory in Jesus, but beware of going beyond it." (enduringword.com)

---

### Denominational and Other Perspectives

**David Guzik (Enduring Word)**, representing a charismatic/Calvary Chapel tradition, emphasises the land as a freely given inheritance, the Christological pointer of Eleazar as High Priest, and the devotional application about contentment with God-given boundaries. (enduringword.com)

**Matthew Henry (Reformed/Puritan)**, quoted extensively in Precept Austin, draws the spiritual lesson that God gives His people only a small share of this world — those who have their portion in heaven should be content with a small pittance of earth. (preceptaustin.org)

**Thomas Constable (Dispensational/Evangelical — Dallas Theological Seminary)** notes the distinction between the Numbers 34 borders and the Genesis 15 borders promised to Abraham, and explains the conditional expansion principle. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-34.html)

**John Gill (Particular Baptist, 18th century)** provides detailed notes on the lots and tribal representation, emphasising God's sovereign ordering of the inheritance through the casting of lots. (mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/34.htm — search excerpt)

**Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran, 19th century)** offer careful philological and geographical analysis, particularly on the Hebrew terms for borders and the identification of sites in the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-34.html)

**JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown)**, a broadly evangelical and Reformed commentary, provides the most detailed geographical identifications, including Mount Hor as "the high double mountain" (Amana) and the Zedad/Sudud connection. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/numbers-34.html)

---

### What I Could Not Find

- **Catholic and Orthodox commentaries**: Searches to newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return results for Numbers 34 specifically within the search limits.
- **Lutheran (LCMS / 1517.org)**: No specific Numbers 34 commentary pages were found.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu)** and **Reformed (ligonier.org, monergism.com)**: No specific Numbers 34 content returned in the search results.
- **Modern scholarly perspectives (bibleodyssey.org)**: Not found in search results. The NET Bible notes were accessible only as translation text, not the full study notes.
- This is a relatively under-commented chapter; most denominational traditions do not produce distinctive readings because the chapter is primarily geographical and administrative. The main area where Protestant traditions differ — the relationship between the Numbers 34 borders and the Genesis 15 Abrahamic promise (whether it is conditional, unconditional, or progressively fulfilled) — is reflected above in the Constable (dispensational) and Reformed (covenantal) approaches.
